'''''Lygodium japonicum''''' is a species of fern that is known by the common names '''Japanese climbing fern''' and '''vine-like fern'''.<ref>{{Cite book|url=http://www.forest.go.kr/kna/special/download/English_Names_for_Korean_Native_Plants.pdf|title=English Names for Korean Native Plants|publisher=[[Korea National Arboretum]]|year=2015|isbn=978-89-97450-98-5|location=Pocheon|pages=530|access-date=4 January 2017|via=[[Korea Forest Service]]|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20170525105020/http://www.forest.go.kr/kna/special/download/English_Names_for_Korean_Native_Plants.pdf|archivedate=25 May 2017}}</ref> It is native to eastern Asia, from Pakistan through India east to Taiwan, Japan, Korea, and south through southeastern Asia to New Guinea.<ref name="POWO">{{cite POWO |title=''Lygodium japonicum'' (Thunb.) Sw. |id=17143040-1 |access-date=2025-07-05}}</ref> The fern is present in the southeastern United States, Puerto Rico, South Africa, and Australia as an introduced species.<ref name="POWO"/>

==Description==
This fern produces a creeping stem from which grow very long leaves, the longest exceeding {{convert|30|m|ft|abbr=off}}.<ref>{{cite book| last= Fayaz | first= Ahmed | date= 2011 | title= Encyclopedia of Tropical Plants | location= Buffalo, New York | publisher= Firefly Books | page= 19 | ISBN=978-1-55407-489-1  }}</ref>  The leaves have [[rachis]]es, which are vine-like and may climb other vegetation. What appear to be individual leaves sprouting from the twining rachis are actually leaflets, which are smaller segments from the main leaf. There are two types of leaflets, sterile and fertile. The sterile frond has lance-shaped segments. The fertile frond has more intricately divided, fringed segments. It is lined with [[sporangia]] on the edges.<ref name=feis>Munger, Gregory T. 2005. [http://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/fern/lygspp/all.html ''Lygodium'' spp.] In: Fire Effects Information System, [Online]. U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Rocky Mountain Research Station, Fire Sciences Laboratory (Producer). Retrieved 11-07-2011.</ref><ref name="fna">[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=200003069 ''Lygodium japonicum''.] Flora of North America. Retrieved 11-07-2011.</ref> The plant reproduces via [[spore]]s and spreads [[vegetative reproduction|vegetatively]] via underground [[rhizome]]s.<ref name=feis/>

==Taxonomy==
The [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''japonicum'', refers to the Latin term for 'being from Japan'.<ref>Allen J. Coombes {{google books|capqDQYT_VYC&|The A to Z of Plant Names: A Quick Reference Guide to 4000 Garden Plants|page=142}}</ref>

It was first published and described as ''Ophioglossum japonicum'' in the family [[Ophioglossaceae]] by [[Carl Peter Thunberg]] in Syst. Veg. edition 14 on page 926 in 1784, before [[Olof Swartz]] reclassified it as ''Lygodium japonicum'' in J. Bot. (edited by Schrader) on page 106 in 1802.<ref>{{cite web|title=Schizaeaceae Lygodium japonicum (Thunb.) Sw.|url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=17143040-1 |publisher=Ipni.org|accessdate=29 December 2017}}</ref><ref name="Plantlst">{{ThePlantList | authority = (Thunb.) Sw. | accessdate = 29 December 2017 }}</ref>

== Invasiveness ==
An introduced species in North America, Japanese climbing fern was first recorded as being established in [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]] in 1903.<ref name=feis/> In the southeastern United States this plant is now considered an invasive weed of economic and ecological significance.<ref name="min">Minogue, P. J., et al. (2010). [http://www.bioone.org/doi/abs/10.1614/IPSM-D-09-00023.1 Japanese climbing fern (''Lygodium japonicum'') management in Florida's Apalachicola bottomland hardwood forests.] ''Invasive Plant Science and Management'' 3(3):246-252. Retrieved 11-07-2011.</ref>

It grows in moist, swampy habitat, especially in disturbed areas. The presence of species such as the [[Boehmeria cylindrica|small-spike false nettle]] (''Boehmeria cylindrica''), [[Osmunda spectabilis|royal fern]] (''Osmunda spectabilis''), [[Pleopeltis polypodioides|resurrection fern]] (''Pleopeltis polypodioides'' ssp. ''polypodioides''), and [[Blechnum serrulatum|toothed midsorus fern]] (''Telmatoblechnum serrulatum'') indicates the likely presence of this species.<ref name=feis/><ref>{{Cite web|title=Telmatoblechnum serrulatum (Rich.) Perrie, D.J.Ohlsen & Brownsey, 2014|url=https://www.gbif.org/species/160291847|access-date=2021-02-11|website=www.gbif.org|language=en}}</ref> During [[controlled burn]]s of wooded areas this fern may act as a "[[fuel ladder]]", which would allow the flames to climb into the canopy and destroy trees. After burns the fern can quickly grow back, so it cannot be controlled by fire.<ref name="min2">Minogue, P. J., et al. [http://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/fr280 Biology and control of Japanese Climbing Fern (''Lygodium japonicum'').] University of Florida IFAS Extension. Retrieved 11-07-2011.</ref>

In Europe, ''Lygodium japonicum'' has been included in the list of Invasive Alien Species of Union concern (the Union list) since 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|title=List of Invasive Alien Species of Union concern - Environment - European Commission|url=https://ec.europa.eu/environment/nature/invasivealien/list/index_en.htm|access-date=2021-07-27|website=ec.europa.eu}}</ref> This implies that this species cannot be imported, cultivated, transported, commercialized, planted, or intentionally released into the environment in the whole of the European Union.<ref>{{Cite web|title=REGULATION (EU) No 1143/2014 of the European parliament and of the council of 22 October 2014 on the prevention and management of the introduction and spread of invasive alien species|url=https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32014R1143&from=EN}}</ref>
